The direct phrasing keeps the contrast between martial arts and science.
SOL keeps the water surging up without the awkward force explanation.
The possessive is clearer; the deputy remains crouched like a shrimp with the others.
“Fired, all right” keeps the speaker’s blunt confirmation and poor-aim criticism.

SOL drops the sacrifice image in the river-wave-pool joke; BASE preserves it.
SOL keeps the narrator’s conclusion in a natural first-person thought.
SOL preserves the warlords’ rise and struggle for supremacy without extra framing.
SOL preserves Hunter as a profession and the soldiers’ resulting laxity.
“Had it in spades” keeps the narrator’s teasing tone and the deputy’s failure to understand.

Dropping “the” before government troops does not change the meaning.

The urgent drums beneath the continuous cannon roar preserve both sounds and their relation.

SOL preserves the noninterference rule and the leader’s vicious, devious reputation.
The speaker’s voice trailing off preserves the fading delivery.
The boat’s silence and the young man’s fading smile remain intact.
SOL adds that the wine splashed across a table; the source only says it splashed chaotically.
“Bearing of wealth and status” naturally conveys the group’s privileged appearance.
The age comparison and the group’s tense attention are preserved.
The young man’s genuine curiosity and pointed question remain.
The merchant remains the first speaker and stammers.
“Regretted opening his mouth” naturally preserves his regret over speaking carelessly.
The Korean says the merchant had seen and heard things; SOL retains only that he heard things.
The late apology’s failure to calm the young man’s temper is preserved.
The eyes regain their usual cunning slant.
The merchant’s bowed posture and the young man’s glare are preserved.
The contrast and the merchant’s complaint about martial-world ruffians remain clear.
SOL’s “they” ambiguously points to the government and Murim, rather than the martial artists the young man despises.
“Hardened that belief” preserves how the earlier event strengthened his view.
“Martial-world ruffians” preserves the source’s meaning and contempt.
The chill in his voice prompts the others to bow hurriedly.
The praise and rhetorical question keep the sycophantic tone.
The courtesans’ fluttering garments and the shift in the mood remain.
The young man still stands apart and looks arrogantly down at the bowed figures.

The terrible memories, lingering anger, and gesture toward the Yangtze remain.
“Shatter before the might” conveys the young man’s boast about the pirates’ defeat.
The simultaneous turn and involuntary blink are preserved.
The first thought is retained without redundant phrasing.

“No, something had changed” preserves the correction and leads into the reveal.
The boat is closing in at great speed, preserving the source’s sudden approach.
The source leaves the second group unspecified; SOL narrows them to guests.
“Come to think of it” preserves the realization.
The ships’ continued firing and increasingly frantic, disordered volleys remain.

The soldiers’ matching claim that they are shooting straight is preserved.
The angry question remains; the removed exclamation marks do not change its force.

The demand for an explanation remains; punctuation does not alter the meaning.
The profanity and the soldier’s exasperated refusal to explain are preserved.
“Meant every word” naturally conveys the sincerity of the curse.
The repeated firing and hundreds of cannonballs launched collectively are preserved.
SOL keeps the poor training, terrible aim, and expectation that at least one shot should hit without BASE’s added “common courtesy.”
Naming the boat clarifies what remains intact.
The vessel still emerges from darkness through the black current like a ghost.
The question remains; the source does not require emphatic punctuation.
Fear rises in everyone alongside the question.

decisions.replacement: Every sailor had heard stories of ghost ships that cannonballs couldn’t sink—and whose dead crews wouldn’t stay dead.

The sight itself horrifies him, preserving the reaction.
“Fucking” intensifies the source’s vulgar exclamation beyond “insane.”
He mutters vulgar words without realizing it, then gapes.
The disbelief at what he sees through the lens is preserved.

“Knocking away” preserves the people’s action against the incoming cannonballs.

The difficulty explaining what he saw and fear of being thought mad remain.
His concern vanishes almost immediately, preserving the transition.
The unforgettable face is spotted through the lens.
Ju Wongong’s strange noises and shout remain in sequence.
The imperial command, self-correction, and claimed imperial kinship remain.
